conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Sarah, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new moms to make sure they’re getting the emotional support they need after baby arrives. Today I’d like to spend a few minutes with you doing the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a short, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything you share is confidential, and my only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported. We’ll go through the questions one by one, and you can answer in whatever way feels most comfortable.

Shall we begin?

Over the past week, when you think about times you were able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how did that feel for you?

Honestly… I can still laugh, especially when my baby does those little funny faces, but it feels kind of muted—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment. Most of the time I’m just tired and the jokes don’t land the same way they used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah... I can still laugh, but it's not the same easy, spontaneous feeling I used to have. Sometimes I have to push myself to smile, and even when something is genuinely funny, the laughter feels kind of forced or fades quickly.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can shower in peace—but the excitement isn’t as big as it used to be. Even outings I normally would’ve loved feel more like chores I have to get through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. The other night she wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking maybe I’m just not doing something right—like if I were a better mom she’d sleep. I’ll replay it in my head even after she finally dozes off. It’s not every hour or anything, but a couple of times this week I’ve ended up in tears because I felt like I’d somehow failed her over little stuff.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A few times, yeah. Like yesterday I suddenly thought, “What if she stops breathing in the crib?” even though her monitor was fine and she was sleeping peacefully. It lasted maybe five minutes, then I could calm myself, but it pops up out of nowhere and makes my chest feel tight until I remind myself she’s okay.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—nothing like a full-blown attack. I do get that quick rush of “what-if” fear, but it’s short and I can settle it pretty fast. So I wouldn’t say I’ve been truly scared or panicky without a reason this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When she cluster-feeds and the laundry’s piled up, it feels like I’m running in circles. I usually manage to get through it, but I’ve had a couple of moments where I just had to put her in the crib for five minutes and step away to breathe.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’ve had trouble drifting off a couple of nights, but it’s more my mind racing about tomorrow’s to-do list than feeling really unhappy. Once I’m asleep I stay asleep—unless she wakes me—so the sleep part’s been okay.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel that way sometimes. It’s not every day, but there have been moments—especially in the late afternoon when I’m tired and she’s fussy—where I just feel this heavy sadness. I’ll sit there rocking her and tears start coming for no real reason. It usually passes after a little while, but it catches me off guard.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, that happened twice this week. Once was when she wouldn’t nap and I couldn’t even get a shower; I just sat on the bed with her and cried for a few minutes. The other time was after a phone call with my mother-in-law—perfectly nice conversation, but I hung up and the tears came. Both times I felt better after I let it out, but I definitely cried because I felt overwhelmed and low.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt tired and weepy, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that, over the past week, laughter feels forced, activities you used to anticipate now feel like chores, and unexpected waves of sadness arrive-especially when fatigue sets in. You've cried twice, questioned your adequacy as a mom, and felt briefly overwhelmed, yet you've also found ways to cope and you consistently deny any wish to harm yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughs less easily and describes forced/fading laughter, matching "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment that's clearly less than before, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports repeated self-blame several times this week, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes spontaneous, intrusive anxious thoughts occurring without cause, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She acknowledges frequent difficulty coping, describing being overwhelmed by daily tasks and needing to step away to breathe, which aligns with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, recurring episodes of sadness that arise "sometimes" and are triggered by daily stressors, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 14 places you above the 13-point threshold where <med>postpartum depression</med> is considered probable and urgent referral is advised. You endorse clear-cut depressive symptoms (<sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>) plus mild <sym>anxiety</sym> without current safety risk. This pattern is consistent with a <med>Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset</med> under <med>DSM-5</med> criteria, pending full diagnostic evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent visit with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss mood, screening results, and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and, if appropriate, <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Arrange practical support-partner, family, or postpartum doula-for night feeds and household tasks so you can obtain 4-6 hours of uninterrupted sleep
4. Use brief self-care strategies: daily outdoor walks, balanced snacks every 3-4 hours, and 5-minute breathing breaks when the baby is safe in the crib
5. Keep the 24-hr <med>Postpartum Support International</med> helpline number (1-800-944-4773) and local emergency services in your phone for immediate support
6. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks or sooner if mood worsens, hopelessness appears, or you ever feel unsafe
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: anonymous postpartum client (approximately 1–2 wks after delivery, per cluster-feeding report)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood: "heavy sadness," tearfulness most days, worse late afternoon (Q8)  
- Anhedonia: diminished laughter/spontaneous enjoyment; formerly pleasant activities feel like chores (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt: self-criticism re infant care; tearful rumination (Q3)  
- Recurrent, intrusive "what-if" worries (e.g., infant breathing) with brief physical tension; no full panic attacks (Q4, Q5)  
- Frequent crying spells (2× this week) triggered by minor stressors; brief relief afterward (Q9)  
- Feeling overwhelmed and "running in circles"; needed to set baby down to breathe (Q6)  
- Mild bedtime racing mind; sleep continuity intact once asleep (Q7)  

Symptoms denied  
- Panic attacks, palpitations, or sustained panic (Q5)  
- Thoughts of self-harm (Q10)  

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms present several days per week, causing subjective distress and minor functional impact (household tasks, enjoyment), without safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for Unspecified Depressive Disorder and/or Unspecified Anxiety Disorder in perinatal context; does not currently meet threshold for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset (no marked impairment, intact sleep duration, no suicidal ideation). Continue monitoring for symptom escalation, functional decline, or emergence of safety risk.

Risk factors  
- Primiparous adjustment stress  
- Social supports limited to occasional maternal help  
- Fatigue/exhaustion cluster-feeding cycle  

Next screening  
Repeat within 2 weeks; educate on emergency contact if mood worsens, hopelessness or self-harm ideas develop; consider referral for supportive counseling and/or psychoeducation on postpartum mood disorders.
